clue.text: Undermine plan that's raised grass

indicators.note: in a down entry, raised means the letters are lifted so they read from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: to sap is to undermine or weaken
a map is a plan or chart

explanation.surface: A saboteur plots to undermine a scheme, and the scheme turns out to involve some tall grass.
explanation.definitionFit: The pampas are the vast grassy plains of South America, and pampas grass is the tall plumed plant named after them.

clue.text: Fool, keeping up badly, massages tummy pain

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word for badly is read from the bottom upwards
the word for fool keeps, or holds, another piece inside it

blocks.note: a mug is a gullible person, a fool
ill means badly, as in ill-treated
rubs, as a verb, means massages

explanation.surface: Someone foolish who copes badly gives a massage to a painful stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tummy pain' could be a symptom, but here it is a single old colloquial word.
explanation.definitionFit: Mulligrubs is an old colloquial word for colic or a stomach ache, and also for a fit of low spirits.

clue.text: Half play a note for love?

indicators.note: only half of the following word is kept, its opening portion

blocks.note: the first half, three of its four letters, rounded up
the tonic is the keynote, the first note of a musical scale

explanation.surface: A musician half-heartedly plays one note as a romantic gesture.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose and question-marked: platonic describes a kind of love, one without sexual desire.
explanation.definitionFit: Platonic love is close affection without romance or desire, named after Plato's account of an ideal friendship.

clue.text: Financial restriction on the Mafia covering the Old Lady in the morning

definitions.text: covering the Old Lady in the morning

indicators.note: in an across entry, one thing placed on another comes after it, so the restriction is sent second

blocks.note: the Mob is a name for the Mafia
a cap is an upper limit on spending or charges

explanation.surface: A spending limit is imposed on organised crime, with a cosy image of granny dressed at breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: The long definition is a description of the object itself, rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A mobcap is a large soft frilled cotton cap formerly worn indoors by women, especially elderly ones, in the morning.

clue.text: Bad fit for French gentleman: cast him out!

definitions.text: Bad fit for French gentleman: cast him out!

blocks.note: surface reading: clothes that do not suit the man wearing them
setter's reading: a Frenchman addressed with the wrong title, a Miss rather than Monsieur, is wrongly paired

explanation.surface: A tailor is told that a garment fits a French gentleman so badly that he should be thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: MIS- is a prefix meaning bad and MATCH means fit; the French gentleman, M, hints at Miss, the wrong title for him.
explanation.definitionFit: A mismatch is a poor pairing, two things that go together badly, such as clothes and wearer.

clue.text: Libel - mud being thrown, by gum!

indicators.note: something thrown is flung about, so these letters land in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims 'by gum!' as libellous mud is slung, mud-slinging being a phrase for smearing a reputation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By gum!' reads as a mild northern English oath; here gum is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Bdellium is an aromatic gum resin from trees related to myrrh, mentioned in the Bible.

clue.text: Leave covering for creature on the lake

blocks.note: fur is the coat covering an animal
lough is the Irish word for a lake

explanation.surface: Some kind of shelter is wanted for an animal living on a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leave' looks like a verb, but it is the noun: time off.
explanation.definitionFit: A furlough is a leave of absence, especially one granted to a soldier or worker.

clue.text: One of many reported, you idiot!

indicators.note: reported means passed on by word of mouth, so the phrase is heard rather than seen

blocks.note: a nit is a fool, so 'you nit' is an insult

explanation.surface: Someone is told off as an idiot, one of many such idiots, it is said.
explanation.walkthrough: Nit is British slang for a silly person, short for nitwit.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit is a single item among a number of identical ones, a single member of a set.

clue.text: Chief under the influence

blocks.note: first meaning: principal or highest
second meaning: intoxicated by drugs

explanation.surface: The boss is drunk or stoned.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means both principal in rank, as in high command, and intoxicated by drugs or drink.

clue.text: Sound start to 23, a 24 for 22 23

blocks.note: first meaning: the opening of the word at 23 sounds like wool, which is what a sheep wears
second meaning: the disguise worn by false prophets, who inwardly are ravening wolves

explanation.walkthrough: The start of WOLVES, WOL, sounds like wool. Matthew 7:15 warns of false prophets which come in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravening wolves.
explanation.definitionFit: Wool is literally a sheep's clothing, and the biblical phrase names the disguise of a predator posing as harmless.

clue.text: See 9
With competent direction, singing about hell by one in employment can bring good out of evil

indicators.note: about means going around, so the word for singing surrounds the word for hell
one is placed in, inside, the word for employment

blocks.note: able means competent
S is south, a compass direction
taken as written
Dis is the classical underworld, and Dante's name for the city of hell
use means employment, as in putting something to use
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A choir with good direction, singing of hell while in work, manages to turn evil into good.
explanation.walkthrough: Hell as Dis comes from Virgil and Dante, where Dis is the lower underworld; the phrase is an everyday English idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: A blessing in disguise is an apparent misfortune that turns out to bring about some good result.

clue.text: Concentration camping on the loch

blocks.note: someone camping is in a tent
Loch Ness is the famous Scottish loch

explanation.surface: The focus needed for a camping holiday beside a Scottish lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concentration camp' runs together in the surface, but concentration is the definition and camping a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Intentness is the state of being intent, fixed closely in attention on something.

clue.text: Plant genetically modified on September the fourth in transport

indicators.note: the date is put in, inside, the word for transport

blocks.note: a car is a means of transport
ult., ultimo, means last month, and the puzzle appeared in October
IV is the Roman numeral for four

explanation.surface: A GM crop is moved by vehicle on 4 September.
explanation.walkthrough: Old business letters dated things like '4th ult.', meaning the fourth of last month; the clue relies on the paper's October date.
explanation.definitionFit: A cultivar is a plant variety produced and maintained by deliberate breeding, a cultivated variety.

clue.text: Hair wrapped round poems from the old country

indicators.note: hair that is wrapped is twisted up, so these letters are twisted into a new order
round means surrounding, so the twisted hair encloses the poems

blocks.note: taken as written
an ode is a lyric poem

explanation.surface: Verses arrive from a homeland, folded inside a lock of hair.
explanation.walkthrough: The old country is literal: Rhodesia is the former name of Zimbabwe.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhodesia was the name of the British colony and later state that became Zimbabwe in 1980, so it is a country no longer.

clue.text: Head girl comes to tea

blocks.note: first meaning: old slang for the head
second meaning: old British slang for an attractive woman

explanation.surface: The head girl of a school is invited round for tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head girl' reads as one school title but splits into two meanings; 'comes to tea' adds a third, as the toasted cake served at teatime.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a griddle cake eaten toasted at tea, dated slang for the head, and dated British slang for women seen as attractive.

clue.text: Game, the first in the "Rising Sun", finished behind the arras

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means the word reads from the bottom upwards
the first is placed in, inside, the other word

blocks.note: polo is a game played on horseback
taken as written
I, one, is the first number in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A game is played at the Rising Sun pub before something is ended behind a tapestry.
explanation.walkthrough: SUN read upwards is NUS, with I inside: NIUS. In Hamlet, Polonius hides behind the arras, a wall tapestry, and is stabbed through it.
explanation.definitionFit: Polonius, the courtier in Hamlet, is killed while eavesdropping behind the arras in Gertrude's chamber.

clue.text: Don't start another meal without striking - it's rude

indicators.note: the meal is told not to begin, so its opening letter is dropped
without in its old sense means outside, so the meal goes around the next piece

blocks.note: lunch is a meal, another besides breakfast
workers who are striking are out

explanation.surface: Starting another meal without hitting anyone first would be bad manners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' seems to mean lacking, but here it means outside: UNCH goes around OUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncouth means lacking good manners or refinement, rude and boorish.

clue.text: Golding's the author capable of prophesy?

indicators.note: to author is to compose, so these letters are composed into something new

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
taken as written

explanation.surface: William Golding is cast as a novelist who can foresee the future.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The author' looks like a description of Golding; author is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone long-sighted sees far ahead, figuratively shows foresight, which is what a prophet does.

clue.text: Painter, soldier and engineer

blocks.note: GI is an American soldier
Nikolaus Otto was the German engineer who developed the four-stroke engine

explanation.surface: A list of jobs: painter, soldier, engineer.
explanation.definitionFit: Giotto di Bondone was an Italian painter of the early Renaissance, known for the Scrovegni Chapel frescoes.

clue.text: Reminder of p-punishment

blocks.note: the stammered initial letter supplies itself
the rod is corporal punishment, as in spare the rod

explanation.surface: Someone stammering at the thought of a beating, a reminder of past punishment.
explanation.definitionFit: A prod is a nudge or prompt, something that reminds a person to act.

clue.text: Holy place where painters go for 'oney?

indicators.note: the apostrophe marks a dropped aitch, cockney fashion, so the same letter goes from the answer's wordplay

blocks.note: read as the place bees go for honey, the setter reusing 'go' from the definition

explanation.surface: Artists head for a sacred spot in search of honey.
explanation.walkthrough: St Ives, in Cornwall, has long been an artists' colony and is named after a saint, hence holy place; the dropped H turns HIVES into its name.
explanation.definitionFit: St Ives is the Cornish seaside town famed as a haven for painters, and the saint's name makes it holy.

clue.text: Bird with broken wing loves dodging hungry predators

indicators.note: something broken is in pieces, so these letters are put together differently
dodging means darting about, so these letters move out of their order

blocks.note: a raven is a large black bird
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An injured bird keeps clear of romance while hungry hunters lurk.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is from Matthew 7:15, on false prophets who are inwardly ravening wolves.
explanation.definitionFit: Ravening means voraciously hunting for prey, and wolves are predators, so the phrase is hungry predators.

clue.text: See 22
See 11
One follows backbones

blocks.note: the stern is the back of a ship
a means one, as in a single item
the printed word is read in two parts, its first half wordplay and its second half the definition

explanation.surface: A single item comes after a set of spines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backbones' looks like one word but splits: back is wordplay and bones the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sterna is the plural of sternum, the breastbone, so the word names a set of bones.
